extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematical researchers and advanced students interested in formulating and solving research problems
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for proposing, formulating, and judging mathematical research problems and their solutions, with emphasis on clarity, rigor, axiomatic foundations, methods, and the balance of difficulty and applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness and ease of comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical problem should be clear and easily comprehended; clearness attracts while the complicated repels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert endorses the maxim that a theory (and even more so a problem) is not complete until it can be explained simply; clear, easily comprehended problems draw attention and workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate difficulty (enticing but accessible)
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem should be sufficiently difficult to entice work, yet not completely inaccessible so as not to mock our efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good problems act as guide-posts on the way to new truths and provide pleasure in successful solution; examples include Bernoulli's brachistochrone and Fermat's problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical usefulness and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems should have deep significance for the advance of mathematical science and play an important role in the work of investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert cites historical examples (e.g., Fermat leading to ideal numbers and the development of algebraic number theory; three-body problem leading to methods in celestial mechanics) to show that apparently special problems can have broad impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of finite verification — exact formulability
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be possible to establish the correctness of a solution by a finite number of steps based upon a finite number of hypotheses which are implied in the problem statement and which must always be exactly formulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the requirement of rigor: correctness must be checkable by a finite logical process and hypotheses must be stated exactly; new problems should be grafted onto established achievements to thrive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor in proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor in proof is a necessary requirement for a perfect solution and corresponds to a universal philosophical necessity of understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigor often leads to simpler, more developable methods; examples include Weierstrass's foundations for the calculus of variations and simplifications in theory of algebraic curves and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact statement of hypotheses / axiomatic clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems must state precisely the hypotheses (axioms) on which they depend; the axioms act as definitions of elementary ideas and nothing is correct unless derived from those axioms by a finite number of logical steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert emphasizes collecting axioms (e.g., arithmetic with completeness/Archimedean axioms) and investigating their independence and compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of impossibility as a legitimate outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: When a problem cannot be solved under given hypotheses, it may be important to show the impossibility of solution under those hypotheses; impossibility proofs are a valid and valuable settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: ancient impossibility results (irrationality proofs), and modern impossibility/independence results (e.g., squaring the circle, parallel postulate variations); proving impossibility can be as significant as producing a constructive answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for general viewpoints and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to solve a problem often stems from not recognizing a more general standpoint from which the problem is a single link; finding this standpoint yields methods applicable to related problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert points to Cauchy's complex integration and Kummer's ideals as examples where a broader perspective produced powerful methods; looking for general methods is the most practicable way forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization and solving simpler subproblems
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialization — finding and solving simpler, related problems — is often more important than seeking sweeping general methods; solving easier problems provides devices and concepts capable of generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert calls this rule a key lever for overcoming difficulties and claims it is used (often unconsciously) by mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction and rigorous grounding of new concepts and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: New concepts require corresponding new signs chosen to remind us of the originating phenomena and must be integrated after rigorous axiomatic investigation of their conceptual content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometrical figures and arithmetical symbols act as mnemonic/graphic formulas but their use as strict proof presupposes precise axioms underlying those figures; invention of symbols should accompany axiomatic clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay between thought (pure mathematics) and experience (applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems may arise from external phenomena or evolve internally by logical combination; both sources are fruitful and their interplay explains analogies across mathematical branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert notes that practical problems open new fields and sometimes lead to answers for old problems; cross-fertilization is a desirable feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom compatibility and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: When investigating foundations, one must ask whether axioms are independent and, above all, whether they are non-contradictory (compatible): i.e., that finite logical steps from the axioms never lead to contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert discusses methods for proving compatibility (e.g., constructing number fields to model geometrical axioms) and his replacement of continuity by Archimedean + completeness axioms as a route to direct proofs of compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical existence via non-contradiction (constructive/axiomatic existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical object 'exists' if assigning attributes to it cannot lead to contradiction through finite logical processes; proving axioms' compatibility proves mathematical existence of systems like the real numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert contrasts existence in this axiomatic, non-contradiction sense with naive enumerative representations; emphasizes logical tenability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desirability of methods that yield simpler, more generalizable proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigorous methods should aim at simplification and at methods capable of development beyond the immediate problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include function-theoretical methods simplifying algebraic curves theory and Weierstrass's work simplifying calculus of variations; rigorous approaches often reveal more widely applicable techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of axiomatizing physical theories mathematically
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical sciences in which mathematics plays an important role (e.g., probability, mechanics) should be treated by axioms, seeking small axiom sets that can be enlarged to specialize into more detailed theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert recommends mathematicians investigate foundations of mechanics and kinetic theory, deriving limiting processes and exploring equivalence of axiom systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate weakening or alteration of standard axioms to discover neighboring theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Study geometries and theories that arise when particular axioms are excluded or modified (e.g., parallel axiom, Archimedean axiom), thereby discovering 'geometries next to Euclidean'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert suggests systematic construction and treatment of alternative geometries (e.g., Lobachevsky, Riemann, Minkowski, non-Archimedean) to illuminate elementary ideas like distance and plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question differentiability assumptions in structural theories (e.g., Lie groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: In theories that assume differentiability (such as Lie's continuous groups), ask whether differentiability is essential or can be derived/avoided, and investigate functional equations without differentiability assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert points to reductions to analytic groups under certain hypotheses and flags functional equations where sole solutions may be nondifferentiable; encourages examining which results survive without differentiability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for results that reveal unifying structures across mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems and their solutions are especially valuable when they disclose unsuspected relations and analogies between previously separate branches, preserving the organic unity of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert argues that development of sharper tools and simpler methods enables individual investigators to traverse branches and that discoveries revealing unity are particularly desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of reliable, modern expository texts to advance interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The lack of reliable modern textbooks can impede interest in a field; producing modern rigorous expositions is important for propagation and development of subjects (example: calculus of variations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert praises recent rigorous treatments (Kneser) as helping reclaim interest in areas like the calculus of variations and enabling clearer presentation of sufficient/necessary conditions.
